-   Current environment

Exposes the gateway as a remote MCP server over the Streamable HTTP transport (JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP, optionally upgrading to Server-Sent Events for streamed responses). Accepts either a WP Engine API key (prefixed “wpe\_”) carrying the mcp scope, scoped to the key’s project, or an Okta JWT with WPEngine-Account and WPEngine-Project headers (Standalone Coworker). A token issued for a support impersonation session is refused with `403`. An API-key caller receives a deprecation notice in the connect instructions and in each tool result’s `_meta["com.wpengine/deprecation"]`. The result’s content is unchanged. Where API keys are disabled, a key still connects, initializes and lists tools, and every tool call returns the tool error `forbidden`. External MCP clients (e.g. Claude Desktop) can instead use interactive OAuth sign-in, discovered through `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1/mcp`. An OAuth access token must grant a scope for each tool it calls: `urn:wpengine:ai:wordpress:rw` for the site, knowledge base and ability tools, and `urn:wpengine:hosting:tools:rw` for the WP Engine account and environment tools. A request whose token lacks the scope returns `403` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="..."` naming the scopes to request: the token’s current scopes plus the one required. An OAuth access token names a person, not an account, so for such a caller the site, ability and search tools (`list_account_sites`, `list_site_abilities`, `run_site_ability` and `search_abilities`) take a required `account_id`. `list_accounts`, offered only to these callers, returns the accounts the person holds that have connected sites. An `account_id` the person does not hold returns the tool error `account_not_found`. An account the person holds that is not enabled for WP Engine AI APIs returns the tool error `entitlement_required`, or `entitlement_unavailable` when that cannot be checked. A person none of whose accounts is enabled is refused with `403` `entitlement_required`, or `account_required` when they hold no account. API-key and Okta callers do not pass `account_id`. Scopes do not apply to API keys or Okta JWTs. The gateway does not preserve MCP session state between requests; clients should not rely on server-side session continuity across calls. The `list_site_abilities`, `search_abilities`, and `run_site_ability` tools additionally require a personal API key when using API-key auth; a project-scoped key resolves no acting user and these tools return an unauthorized error. Okta JWT callers use the verified subject instead. For `run_site_ability`, a timed-out read returns the tool error code `timeout`, including when WordPress reports an upstream timeout with a REST 504 response. Any WordPress error code and message are retained in the tool error message. Retrying the identical read is safe. An uncertain write returns `ambiguous_outcome` and must not be retried automatically. An account-wide `search_abilities` with no connected sites returns `found: false` and `reason: no_connected_sites` for OAuth and Okta callers, with `help` and `next_steps` directing the client to list sites with pagination and ask the user which site to connect. It does not select a connection URL implicitly. Personal API keys with no active connection receive the same selection guidance in a `not_personally_connected` tool error. `list_account_sites` includes `requires_https` on each site, computed from the recorded site URL on that page, so a client can skip sites that cannot start a personal connection without another lookup. Site-specific calls return guidance for the selected site. Site abilities publish their own input and output schemas through discovery. When available, `wp-engine-ai/search-content` performs literal search of editable stored content and REST-exposed custom fields, rather than relevance-ranked knowledge-base search. Matching ignores letter case by default; set `case_sensitive: true` for exact case. Each call visits up to 200 posts subject to work and result limits. Pass its returned `next_cursor` as `cursor` with the same query, case mode, scope and limit until `complete` is true; an empty page does not imply completion. Each ability response returns up to 100 occurrences by default, with a maximum of 200 occurrences and 100,000 encoded JSON bytes, excluding the MCP transport envelope. Every literal occurrence, including overlaps, produces a result with a zero-based Unicode character `match_offset` within its stored string leaf and a preview. Field identities can repeat at different offsets. Incomplete pages have `totals: null`. Cursors use compact unpadded base64url and must be copied unchanged, including letter case, with the original limit and search options. The final page has cumulative `totals` across all pages: `matched_posts`, `matched_fields`, and `occurrences`, even when its `matches` is empty. Separate metadata rows count as separate matching fields. Summaries should use these totals verbatim rather than recounting generated tables. Search results identify update targets, not replacement values or a snapshot of the site. When available, `wp-engine-ai/replace-content` applies an approved literal, case-sensitive, non-overlapping replacement to stored post content and/or manual excerpts. Send `ids`, `find` and `replace`; optional `fields` defaults to `["content"]`. Explicitly select `["excerpt"]` for excerpts only or `["content","excerpt"]` for both. Only changed selected fields are written, together per post. A changed field that the post endpoint does not accept fails that post with `unknown_fields` before any selected field is saved. Core pages expose writable REST excerpts even without editor excerpt support. Custom types/controllers must expose the selected field. Generated excerpts, meta/custom fields and ACF are not replaced. Empty, duplicate or unsupported field selections reject the request before reads or writes. An empty replacement deletes the text. Search for equivalent targets with the same `fields` and `case_sensitive: true`. `wp-engine-ai/manage-posts` applies the same status, categories and/or tags to explicit `ids`, with no action selector or replacement inputs. `categories` and `tags` replace complete sets. Each category/tag list accepts at most 100 input entries before deduplication. Over-limit lists reject the entire request before reads or writes. Larger incremental tag changes can be split across calls; never split full-set category/tag replacements, since each call replaces the complete set. Use `tags_add` to add existing tag IDs or `tags_remove` to remove only those IDs, preserving all unrelated tags. Both delta fields may be combined with each other or status/categories, but not with `tags`; overlapping addition/removal IDs reject the request before writes. Already-present additions and absent removals are unchanged without a write. Tag deltas require a writable REST-visible tags field and term assignment permissions. Non-mutating PATCH probes honor matched REST route permissions and REST policy filters before each native tag operation without running the controller’s full-set save. A failed entry with `partial: true` means some changes may already have landed; inspect current state before retrying. No rollback is performed. Ordinary PATCH errors are potentially partial too: core fields can save before a later operation fails. Authorized read-back verifies status/term values; content and excerpt differences are not compared because WordPress save filters may alter them. Unavailable verification is explicitly reported with `diagnostics_truncated`; zero `not_applied_count` then is not proof that requested values landed. Both tools accept at most 50 positive integer ID entries per call. Deduplicate `search-content` match IDs after collecting every page and split approved IDs into batches. Both check a 10-second cooperative budget before starting each post. After expiry, remaining IDs are `failed` with reason `not_attempted`, included in `failed_count`, and were not read or written. Completed outcomes are preserved. Submit only those unattempted IDs in a new approved call, never replay the entire batch. Catchable unexpected site errors also stop the batch: completed outcomes remain, the interrupted post fails with `execution_failed` or `wp_fatal_error`, and later IDs are `not_attempted`. A started write makes the interrupted post potentially partial with unverified, truncated diagnostics. Expected WordPress error responses remain per-post failures. A started post normally finishes its mutation and verification before the next deadline check. A blocking save hook/controller or shorter host/gateway timeout can still prevent a result envelope; inspect current state instead of automatically retrying that ambiguous outcome. Invalid IDs and unsupported fields reject the batch before writes; individual permission or save failures do not roll back other posts. Already-matching values are returned as `unchanged` without a write. Both require an editable supported post type and recheck each ID. Inspect per-post `not_applied_count` and `not_applied` for requested status or terms ignored or changed on save. Full result envelopes are capped at 100,000 encoded bytes, retaining all IDs, outcomes and counts. `diagnostics_truncated` marks shortened diagnostics, `values_truncated` marks shortened requested/stored value previews within a diagnostic entry, and `diagnostics_error` reports unavailable diagnostics. Never retry changed IDs to retrieve diagnostics; replacement is not necessarily idempotent. Search results do not authorize writes. Fresh content is read at execution, but there is no snapshot or atomic conflict guard. Site-written strings and object keys in `run_site_ability`, `get_site_knowledge_base`, `search_knowledge_base`, and `fetch_knowledge_base_document` results have invisible characters removed. Each serialized result is limited to 128 KiB. Larger results are replaced with `{"result_truncated":true,"excerpt":"... [tool result truncated]"}`; the excerpt is a JSON prefix, not a complete document. Error messages are similarly cleaned and limited to 16 KiB of JSON-encoded text.

string

**Agent-Session-Id**

string

Optional. The agent session a site or knowledge-base tool call is being performed for, when the call answers a tool request from that session. ### 403

[](#403)

-   Current environment

Registers a WordPress site with the AI Gateway, or updates an existing registration for the same site. The caller must authenticate with a WP Engine oauth-ext access token obtained via Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591). The gateway returns a stable site\_id for the logical site; client\_id continues to identify the current OAuth registration. Re-registering the same OAuth client updates its metadata in place. Request body is capped at 64 KiB. Unknown JSON fields are rejected. Returns 409 if the token’s account\_id differs from the account that originally registered the client\_id (ownership conflict), or if an existing client moves to a site\_url already owned by another site in the same account.

-   Current environment

Appends one or more events to a session and returns them with assigned ids. The processed\_at timestamp is null until the event is processed by an agent run. Accepts user.message, system.message, and user.tool\_result events, plus user.interrupt to stop a response in progress. A user.interrupt event may be sent by itself with content omitted or set to an empty array. It never starts a run. It requests cancellation of the exact run in flight when the event is accepted; if no run is in flight, the event is still appended and otherwise has no effect. Other runtime-control types (user.tool\_confirmation, user.custom\_tool\_result, user.define\_outcome) are rejected with 400. Sending a user.message starts the session’s agent running asynchronously; this response echoes the events persisted (which may include a synthetic cancellation; see below) and does not contain the agent’s reply. Retrieve the reply and status by listing events (GET /v1/sessions/{session\_id}/events). A single request carries either user.tool\_result events or a user.message/system.message, never both; mixing them is rejected with 400. While a run is in flight and the session is paused awaiting a client tool\_result, a user.message or system.message is rejected with 400 — send the tool\_result first. If no run holds the session, the message resolves the pause instead: the gateway prepends a synthetic user.tool\_result with error\_code “cancelled” for each outstanding tool\_use, then persists your message, so a session whose client went away mid-tool can be continued. A synthetic cancellation does not establish whether the tool executed; read the affected state back before repeating a possibly executed write. Submit tool\_result promptly: a batch containing only distinct results for calls already cancelled this way is rejected with 409, even if newer calls are pending. Unknown IDs, duplicate IDs, or cancelled results mixed with current results or messages are rejected with 400. Asynchronous agent execution is rolling out; until it is enabled for your site, this endpoint stores and echoes the submitted events without producing agent replies. Accepts a service-token bearer authenticating a site or an API key, either of which must be authorized for the session’s project, or a browser session token holding the session\_events scope (bound to the session’s agent and, when the session records an owner\_id, to that same visitor).

**type**

required

Event type. Input events you send include user.message, system.message, user.tool\_result, and user.interrupt. As the agent responds, the session also produces agent.message replies, agent.tool\_use when the agent calls a tool, and status events: session.status\_running, session.status\_idle, and session.error. The session may also produce session.compaction events: when the conversation approaches the model’s context window, the oldest turns are summarized into a session.compaction event whose content is a single text block (the summary). Original events are retained; the summary only changes what the model is replayed on subsequent turns. Finally, each kept agentic-loop turn produces a session.turn\_usage event reporting that turn’s token usage.

string

Allowed values: user.message user.tool\_result user.interrupt system.message agent.message agent.tool\_use session.status\_running session.status\_idle session.error session.compaction session.turn\_usage

**content**

required

Array of content blocks. For user.message, system.message, and agent.message these are message content blocks (for example text, image, or document). For agent.tool\_use the blocks are tool\_use objects with type, id, name, and input fields. For user.tool\_result they are tool\_result objects with tool\_use\_id, content, and is\_error; a failed one additionally carries error\_code (the same bounded value as the event-level error\_code field) and a content body holding a JSON error envelope — an object with a single “error” key whose value has code, message, an optional field naming the offending argument when exactly one is at fault, and retryable indicating whether repeating the identical call may succeed. Reading the envelope rather than the prose is what lets a consumer distinguish “correct this argument” from “try again in a moment”. A successful tool\_result the gateway answered itself may instead carry status, currently only tool\_loaded: the model named a tool that was declared on its agent but not yet in its tool list, so the tool was loaded and nothing was executed for that block. The model’s real call to the same tool follows on a later turn, so a consumer rendering a transcript can present the pair as loading that tool rather than as one call made twice. status is absent from every ordinary tool\_result. For user.interrupt, content is an empty array. For session.status\_idle the content carries a stop\_reason: end\_turn when the turn completed, user\_cancelled when a user.interrupt stopped the run, or client\_tool\_use when the run paused waiting for the client to execute a tool; when stop\_reason is client\_tool\_use, the content also carries a tool\_use\_ids array listing the pending client tool call IDs. When stop\_reason is client\_tool\_use, the content may also carry tool\_traceparents: a map from each pending tool\_use\_id to a W3C traceparent the client can echo on tool\_result for session trace correlation (optional; absent on older gateways). The content also carries context\_tokens: the total token count (input + output) of the run’s most recent turn, reflecting the session’s current context footprint (since each turn resends the full history as input) — useful for warning a user before the conversation approaches the model’s context window. context\_tokens is always present, including 0 when the cycle made no model request. It remains supported. The latest session.turn\_usage event’s total\_tokens is that last kept turn’s own footprint, with the rest of that turn’s usage alongside it, and is the better source for a new integration. After a cycle that compacted, idle context\_tokens is the post-compaction estimate instead — the turn event is not rewritten. For session.turn\_usage the content is a single block reporting one kept agentic-loop turn’s usage as that turn’s model request completed: turn (the turn’s position in the run, from 1), model (the model that served it), input\_tokens, output\_tokens, cache\_read\_input\_tokens, cache\_creation\_input\_tokens, reasoning\_tokens, total\_tokens, and credits\_nano. Providers do not separate tool-call and tool-result tokens from the prompt and completion counts, so neither does this shape. credits\_nano here prices that kept request and is informational: a run cycle is charged once, and the charge is the credits\_nano in the usage object on the cycle’s session.status\_idle or session.error event. Summing the per-turn figures can differ from that charge by rounding and by tokens spent on a citation rescue retry that did not become a kept turn. When a turn stopped early (it reached the output limit or the context limit, the model’s response was blocked by a content filter, it came back empty, or the user cancelled it) and dropped content as a result, the block also carries a discarded object listing what was dropped: reason (max\_tokens, context\_exceeded, content\_blocked, empty\_response, or cancelled), block\_count (how many blocks were dropped), and blocks (the last 20 of them: content blocks in turn order, then any tool calls the provider stream cut off), each with type (for example tool\_use or thought), tool (the tool name, on tool\_use blocks only, up to 128 characters) and chars (its approximate size in characters, not comparable across providers or between complete and cut-off blocks). It lists types, tool names and sizes only, never the content, and is absent when the turn dropped nothing. For session.error the content carries a single block with type “error”, a client-safe text message, a machine-readable code: upstream\_error (the model provider returned an error), rate\_limit\_error (the model provider is temporarily rate limited), context\_exceeded (the conversation exceeded the model’s context window and automatic compaction could not recover), upstream\_timeout (the model provider took too long to respond), max\_iterations (the agent exhausted its model-turn budget without completing the task; retry with a smaller task), max\_tokens (the model hit its output limit; any partial agent.message precedes the error), empty\_response (the model produced no user-visible content after bounded retries), content\_policy\_violation (the model could not produce a response because it may conflict with the content policy), invalid\_tool\_schema (the model rejected a tool definition for this session; retrying the same model often fails), toolset\_incomplete (the agent declares tools the gateway could not resolve — for example a knowledge\_base collection that no longer exists; the run is stopped rather than continued with a partial toolset, and retrying will not help until the agent’s tools\[\] is corrected), run\_timeout (the run’s overall time budget expired before the agent finished; send the message again, ideally as a smaller task), run\_interrupted (the run was cut short before it finished; send the message again), run\_abandoned (the run’s worker was lost before it finished and the run was settled afterwards; send the message again), or internal\_error (an unexpected failure on our side); and an optional request\_id correlating the failure with support-facing logs, present whenever one could be resolved for the request that triggered it. For session.compaction the content is a single text block (the summary) — original events are retained; the summary only changes what the model is replayed on subsequent turns. When the request passed include\_thinking=true, an agent.message produced with reasoning\_effort set may begin with a thought block: type “thought”, a text field holding the model’s reasoning summary, and optionally extra\_content.gateway.thinking\_ms — the measured reasoning duration in milliseconds. Models that reason without exposing the text yield thought blocks with an empty text field and only the duration metadata. Without include\_thinking (the default), thought blocks are omitted from event content. On an agent.message reply grounded in a knowledge base, text blocks may carry a `citations` array listing KB source documents the model referenced. Each citation is an object with `type` (string discriminator — `"knowledge_base"` today; new source kinds may add values in the future), `document_uri` (string, the click-through URL) and `document_title` (string, the human-readable label). The array is optional, including when the reply is based on retrieved content. Consumers rendering a bottom-of-message Sources list should walk all text blocks, dedupe by `document_uri`, and render one link per unique source. Citations provide answer-level attribution, not verification of individual claims. Consumers should read the final event’s citations rather than treating all retrieved documents as answer sources.

-   Current environment

Partially updates an existing agent. Fields omitted from the request body are left unchanged. When updating the model, the new model must support the `tools` capability; models without this capability return HTTP 400. Accepts a service-token bearer authenticating a site or an API key, either of which must be authorized for the agent’s project; reassigning `project_id` requires authorization for the new project too, and it cannot be cleared.

package main
import (  "fmt"  "strings"  "net/http"  "io")
func main() {
  url := "https://api.ai.wpengine.com/v1/sessions/example"

  res, _ := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
  defer res.Body.Close()  body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
  fmt.Println(res)  fmt.Println(string(body))
}

name: Site and WordPress account connections
markdown:
A WordPress site reaches WP Engine AI through two separate connections, made by different people at different times.

A **site connection** puts the site in your account. It is made once, by whoever administers the site, and it is what makes the site visible to everyone on the account.

A **WordPress account connection** is yours alone. You only need one **if you want to run WordPress abilities or manage the site** — from Coworker in WP Engine AI, or from an MCP client like Claude Code. Everything else works without it: listing your sites, reading site metadata, and searching a site’s knowledge base all work as soon as the site is connected.

If you never intend to have an agent act on a site, you can stop after the site connection.

## Overview

[](#overview)

Connection

Who makes it

What it grants

Needed for

**Site connection**

The site’s administrator, once

The site is visible to the whole account

`list_account_sites`, the knowledge base tools

**WordPress account connection**

Each person, per site

That person may run abilities _as their own WordPress user_

`list_site_abilities`, `run_site_ability`, `search_abilities`, Coworker site actions

The second connection is per person, not per account. Connecting a site grants nobody the ability to act on it — including the administrator who connected it.

## Site connection

[](#site-connection)

### What it is

[](#what-it-is)

The site is registered to your account. This happens when the site’s administrator installs the WP Engine AI plugin and completes the registration flow.

### What it gives you

[](#what-it-gives-you)

-   The site appears in `list_account_sites`
-   Site metadata: URL, display name, status
-   Knowledge base access — `get_site_knowledge_base`, `search_knowledge_base`, and `fetch_knowledge_base_document` — where the knowledge base is enabled

### What it does not give you

[](#what-it-does-not-give-you)

Running abilities needs the second connection. Until you make one:

-   `list_site_abilities` returns `not_personally_connected`
-   `run_site_ability` returns `not_personally_connected`

An HTTP site returns `site_requires_https` instead, with no Connect link. `list_account_sites` sets `requires_https` on each site from its URL, so that is visible before either tool is called.

A site connection is _account_\-scoped. If ten people share the account, all ten see the site — and none of them can act on it until each has connected their own WordPress account.

## WordPress account connection

[](#wordpress-account-connection)

### What it is

[](#what-it-is-1)

You have completed the **Connect WordPress Account** consent flow, started from that site’s WordPress admin. That links three things:

-   Your identity, from the user authenticated with OAuth
-   The site
-   Your WordPress user on that site

From then on, abilities you trigger run **as your WordPress user**, with exactly the permissions that user has.

### When you need one

[](#when-you-need-one)

Only for acting on a site:

-   Running WordPress abilities from Coworker in WP Engine AI
-   Running them from an MCP client — `list_site_abilities`, `run_site_ability`, `search_abilities`

You do not need one to list sites, read site metadata, or search a knowledge base.

### How to make one

[](#how-to-make-one)

The flow starts in WordPress admin and finishes in WP Engine AI, so expect to be signed in to both.

1.  Ask for your sites’ connection status, or call `list_account_sites`.
    
2.  For any site with no `wp_connection_status` at all, the answer carries a link. Open it while logged in to that site’s WordPress admin. If no link comes back, build it from the site URL:
    
    `{site_url}/wp-admin/admin.php?page=power-overview&action=trigger_wp_connection`
    
    Opening this link is the only way to start the connection — there is no option to start it manually anywhere in WordPress.
    
3.  WordPress hands you to WP Engine AI, signing you in if you aren’t already. Review the permissions on the consent screen there.
    
4.  Confirm with **Connect WordPress User**. You land back in wp-admin, now connected.
    

![Screenshot: Connect your WordPress account consent screen in WP Engine AI](/_astro/wp-level2-consent.DvR_ySTC_Z10p1ty.webp)

Once per site, per person. The connection lasts until you revoke it in WordPress admin, your WordPress user is deleted, or your account loses access to the site.

### Why it is separate

[](#why-it-is-separate)

WordPress abilities can publish posts, delete users, install plugins, change settings, and read private data. Keeping this connection separate and personal buys three things:

-   **Explicit consent** — nobody acts on a site on your behalf until you say so
-   **Real user identity** — abilities run as your WordPress user, so your role and capabilities still apply, and the site’s logs name you rather than a service account
-   **No blast radius from a shared credential** — no one can act on a site as another person

The gateway checks the connection on every ability call, so a site you have not authorized stays untouchable.

## Connection states

[](#connection-states)

`list_account_sites`, called by a user authenticated with OAuth, reports `wp_connection_status` for each site:

Status

Meaning

What to do

`connected`

Both connections are in place

Nothing — you can run abilities

`needs_reconnect`

Your connection went stale

[Re-authorize](/docs/ai/api/mcp/troubleshooting/#it-worked-yesterday-and-now-says-the-connection-is-stale)

`site_requires_https`

The site is not served over HTTPS, so no connection can be made

Enable SSL on the site first

_(omitted)_

You never connected, or the connection was revoked

[Make the connection](#how-to-make-one)

There is no `not_connected` value — when you have no usable connection the field is **absent from the response entirely**. Absence is therefore ambiguous on its own: it cannot distinguish “never connected” from “revoked”.

`needs_reconnect` shows up when your WordPress credentials changed, the site invalidated its sessions, or the connection was flagged for reauthorization. The fix is the same as making it the first time — [How to make one](#how-to-make-one), opening the link while logged in to wp-admin.

## What each credential can reach

[](#what-each-credential-can-reach)

Credential

Sees

Can act on

**User authenticated with OAuth**

Every site in your account

Sites where _you_ connected your WordPress account

**User API key**

Every site in your account

Sites where _you_ connected your WordPress account

**Account API key**

Every site in your account

Nothing — an account key has no acting user

An account API key can list sites and search knowledge bases, but it resolves no WordPress user, so it can never run an ability.

API keys on MCP are deprecated. Where a server refuses API keys, every tool returns `forbidden`, so a key sees and acts on nothing.

## Worked example

[](#worked-example)

1.  **Alice’s team connects `example.com`** to their account. The site is now visible to everyone on the account. Alice calls `list_account_sites` and sees `example.com` listed with no `wp_connection_status` field on it.
    
2.  **Alice connects her WordPress account** for `example.com`, because she wants Coworker to draft posts there. She opens the connect link while logged in to wp-admin and authorizes the gateway to act as her WordPress user.
    
3.  **Alice runs an ability.** `run_site_ability` creates a post; the gateway checks her connection first, the ability executes as her WordPress user, and the site’s logs show the post was created by Alice.
    
4.  **Bob, on the same team, tries the same thing.** He gets `not_personally_connected` — the site connection is shared, his WordPress account connection is not. Bob connects his own, or carries on using the site’s knowledge base without one.
    

* * *

#### Making the connection

-   [Connect Claude Code — a full setup path, including your WordPress account](/docs/ai/api/mcp/how-to/configure-claude-code/)
-   [Authentication — MCP clients authenticate with OAuth](/docs/ai/api/authentication/#mcp-clients-authenticate-with-oauth)
-   [Troubleshooting — fixes by symptom](/docs/ai/api/mcp/troubleshooting/)

name: Stream a chat completion
Using the WordPress AI Client
markdown:
If you’re building a WordPress plugin or theme, you may not need to call the AI API directly. WordPress 7.0 ships a built-in [AI Client](https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/03/24/introducing-the-ai-client-in-wordpress-7-0/) with a fluent PHP API for text, image, and speech generation, and the WP Engine AI Connector plugin registers a `wpengine` provider for it — so your code never touches an API key, and auth, retries, and provider routing are handled for you.

## Prerequisites

[](#prerequisites)

1.  Install and activate the [WP Engine AI Connector](https://wp-product-info.wpesvc.net/v1/plugins/wpe-ai-connector?download) and [WP Engine AI](https://wp-product-info.wpesvc.net/v1/plugins/wpe-hub?download) plugins.
2.  From **Settings → Connectors → WP Engine AI Connector**, connect the site to a WP Engine account.
3.  Run WordPress 7.0 or later. The AI Client is part of WordPress core, so your plugin or theme calls it directly — there is nothing extra to install.

No API key in code

Once the connector is connected to a WP Engine account, it handles authentication automatically on every request. There is no `Authorization` header for you to set.

## What it looks like

[](#what-it-looks-like)

Generate text with the fluent builder. The AI Client picks a suitable model from the registered providers, sends the request through the connector, and returns the generated text.

```
<?phpdeclare( strict_types = 1 );
$summary = wp_ai_client_prompt( 'Summarize the speed of light in one sentence.' )    ->using_system_instruction( 'You are concise.' )    ->using_temperature( 0.2 )    ->generate_text();
if ( is_wp_error( $summary ) ) {    // Log the error and fall back to a non-AI code path.    return;}
```

`generate_text()` returns a `string` on success and a `WP_Error` on failure — `wp_ai_client_prompt()` converts every AI Client exception into a `WP_Error`, so always check the result with `is_wp_error()`. For the full result object (token usage, the model that answered, finish reason) use `generate_text_result()` instead. The `wpengine` provider returns one candidate per request, so ask for a single result rather than several via `generate_texts()`.

Pin specific models when you need them for cost, latency, or capability reasons. List them in order of preference — the AI Client uses the first one the connector exposes:

```
$summary = wp_ai_client_prompt( 'Summarize the speed of light in one sentence.' )    ->using_provider( 'wpengine' )    ->using_model_preference( 'google/gemini-3.5-flash', 'google/gemini-3.7-flash' )    ->generate_text();
```

Without a preference, the connector uses the model chosen on its settings screen (Claude Sonnet 5.5 by default). If that model can’t handle the prompt, it falls back to the newest Claude Sonnet, then Haiku, then Fable, then Gemini Flash. Web search works on Claude and on Gemini 3 and newer; Gemini can only block domains, so a web search that sets allowed domains needs a Claude model. Structured output (a JSON schema) needs Gemini, because the Claude models return text only. Reorder that chain with the `wpe/ai/connector/fallback_models` filter:

```
add_filter(    'wpe/ai/connector/fallback_models',    function ( array $models ): array {        // Try Haiku before Sonnet.        usort(            $models,            fn ( string $a, string $b ): int =>                (int) str_contains( $b, 'claude-haiku-' ) <=> (int) str_contains( $a, 'claude-haiku-' )        );
        return $models;    });
```

The filter orders models; it can’t exclude them. Any model the connector offers that isn’t in the chain still comes after it, so removing one from the chain only moves it down the list. The order is stored with the cached model list, so a change takes effect after the connector settings are saved, the plugin is updated, or the cache expires (24 hours).

The connector reports itself as unavailable when the site isn’t connected, when the current request isn’t allowed to use the connection (see [Who can make requests](#who-can-make-requests)), and for about a minute after WP Engine AI fails to list its models. Check that before showing an AI feature, so the feature is hidden instead of surfacing an error. WordPress core doesn’t wrap this check, so call the bundled SDK class directly:

```
use WordPress\AiClient\AiClient;
if ( ! AiClient::isConfigured( 'wpengine' ) ) {    // Show an admin notice or fall back to a non-AI code path.    return;}
```

Swap `generate_text()` for `generate_image()` to produce an image instead. It returns a `WordPress\AiClient\Files\DTO\File` whose image data is inline and base64-encoded. Decode it to save the image to the uploads directory:

```
$image = wp_ai_client_prompt( 'A pixel-art lighthouse at sunset' )    ->using_provider( 'wpengine' )    ->generate_image();
if ( is_wp_error( $image ) ) {    return;}
// $image->getMimeType() reports the format, e.g. image/png.$upload = wp_upload_bits(    'lighthouse.png',    null,    base64_decode( $image->getBase64Data() ));
```

## Who can make requests

[](#who-can-make-requests)

The connector only attaches the site’s credentials to a request when it runs as one of:

-   A logged-in user with the `edit_posts` capability (Contributor and above)
-   WP-CLI
-   WP-Cron

For any other request — including one made while rendering a page for an anonymous visitor — `AiClient::isConfigured( 'wpengine' )` returns `false` and the connector is skipped when WordPress picks a model. A call pinned to the connector with `using_provider( 'wpengine' )` returns a `WP_Error` instead of reaching WP Engine AI.

To allow other requests, filter `wpe_ai_connector_authorize_request`. The filter also decides whether the connector is offered at all: it is called with a `GET` request to `v1/models` for that check, so a filter that inspects the request URL must allow that request too.

```
add_filter(    'wpe_ai_connector_authorize_request',    function ( bool $authorized ): bool {        return $authorized || my_plugin_can_use_ai();    });
```

Every authorized request uses the site’s credits

Authorizing anonymous visitors lets anyone who can reach that code path spend the site’s AI credits. Put your own rate limiting or abuse protection in front of any public-facing AI feature.

## Connector Approvals

[](#connector-approvals)

Sites can also restrict which plugins use the connector. The [WordPress AI plugin](https://wordpress.org/plugins/ai/) has an optional Connector Approval experiment, off by default. When a site admin turns it on, calls from a plugin that hasn’t been approved to use the `wpengine` connector return a `WP_Error` with the code `prompt_network_error` and a message saying the connector has not been approved for that plugin. The blocked plugin then appears as a pending request under **Tools → Connector Approvals**, where an admin can approve it.

## What it doesn’t cover

[](#what-it-doesnt-cover)

The AI Client is a provider-agnostic content-generation layer, not a full AI API client. It’s built to work against any registered AI provider, so it only exposes generation primitives generic enough to make sense across providers — it has no method surface for:

-   Token counting, transcription, image alt-text, content summarization, or taxonomy suggestion
-   Usage analytics or credit balance
-   Site registration or connection management (handled entirely by the AI Connector plugin, not the AI Client)
-   Agents, sessions, or knowledge base collections
-   The MCP transport used by external clients like Claude Code

For any of those, call the [AI API](/docs/ai/api/) directly — see the [API reference](/docs/ai/api/reference/) for every operation.

Where to learn more

The AI Client also supports speech and text-to-speech generation with the same fluent surface. See [Introducing the AI Client in WordPress 7.0](https://make.wordpress.org/core/2026/03/24/introducing-the-ai-client-in-wordpress-7-0/) for the full builder API and provider model — that announcement post is the authoritative reference for the AI Client’s method surface, not this page.

* * *

#### Going beyond the AI Client

-   [API reference — every operation the AI Client does not wrap](/docs/ai/api/reference/)
-   [Getting started — call the API directly](/docs/ai/api/getting-started/)
-   [Authentication — the key the gateway expects](/docs/ai/api/authentication/)

name: Smart Search AI
markdown:
Smart Search AI is a turnkey AI-powered search solution for WordPress. It combines full-text search with AI-powered semantic search, surfacing relevant results based on meaning and context rather than exact keyword or phrase matches. Smart Search AI runs on managed infrastructure, which allows site content to be continuously indexed without sacrificing speed. It is available to all sites built on WordPress, regardless of hosting provider.

[Getting Started with the Smart Search API](/docs/smart-search/getting-started/)Authenticate and make your first request to the Smart Search AI GraphQL API.

[Smart Search AI Architecture](/docs/smart-search/architecture/)How Smart Search AI is built and how the components fit together.

[Support Guide for Smart Search AI](https://wpengine.com/support/wp-engine-smart-search/)Setup details, troubleshooting tips, and product basics.

## Configure Search Behavior

[](#configure-search-behavior)

Use the WordPress dashboard to adjust how Smart Search AI matches content across full-text, semantic, and hybrid models.

-   **Full-text Search**: Select **Stemming** to reduce search terms to their root forms or **Fuzzy Search** to handle typos and minor spelling variations automatically.
-   **[AI-Powered Hybrid Search](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/semantic-search-config/)**: Combines traditional full-text exact matching with semantic search. Use the balance slider to adjust the ratio between keyword matching and semantic context.
-   **Semantic Search**: Uses semantic similarity to surface relevant content even when exact search terms aren’t found.

## Customize Search Results

[](#customize-search-results)

Manually control search outputs to highlight priority content, manage promotions, and define term synonyms.

-   **[Custom Search Results](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/find#custom-search-results)**: Specify exact search terms in WordPress to override standard algorithmic results and return a manually curated set of pages or posts.
-   **[Search Promotions](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/find#promoted-documents)**: Pin key landing pages, products, or promotional content to the top of search result lists using drag-and-drop.
-   **[Synonyms Engine](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/synonyms/)**: Group equivalent keywords and acronyms (e.g., “jacket” and “coat”) so query terms resolve to unified content pools without requiring site content changes.
-   **[Field weighting & prioritization](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/find#field-weighting)**: Assign custom priority weights to specific post titles, body content, taxonomies, and custom fields to promote high-value data in results.

## Integrations

[](#integrations)

Includes native support for WordPress tools, custom APIs, and external data sources. Works with any WordPress installation and hosting provider. Indexing and queries run on dedicated infrastructure, reducing load on your WordPress server.

-   **Hosting agnostic** - Not limited to WP Engine-hosted sites. Available to all WordPress sites, regardless of hosting provider.
-   **Native ACF & WooCommerce support**: Out-of-the-box compatibility with Advanced Custom Fields (ACF & ACF Pro) and native WooCommerce product schemas without manual data mapping.
-   **API-first**: Expose search results, filters, and facets programmatically across a [custom theme](/docs/smart-search/plugin/hooks/) or [custom frontend](/docs/smart-search/getting-started/).
-   **[External data indexing](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/indexing/)**: Index content from external sources outside WordPress, such as custom APIs, databases, or third-party systems.

## Advanced Features

[](#advanced-features)

Additional capabilities for extended indexing formats, frontend search controls, AI agent integration, and analytics.

-   **Faceted Filtering**: Enable taxonomy filters (checkboxes or dropdowns) and numeric range sliders with auto-reloading search results.
-   **[Multimodal & Asset Indexing](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/content-extraction-api/) Beta**: Index text from PDF attachments and image metadata alongside posts and pages.
-   **[Model Context Protocol (MCP) server](/docs/smart-search/mcp/) Beta**: Connect live site content directly to external AI agents (such as Claude or ChatGPT) as a live knowledge base.
-   **[Search Insights & Analytics](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/insights/)**: Access search query volume, popular terms, and zero-result queries directly from the WP Engine User Portal to optimize synonyms and content.

### Looking for support?

Find additional resources in our Support Center, or log in to chat with our support team.

[Visit Support Center](https://wpengine.com/support)[Contact Support](https://my.wpengine.com/support)

name: Smart Search AI Architecture
markdown:
Smart Search AI is a managed search platform for WordPress, headless websites, and custom applications. The Smart Search AI plugin connects WordPress sites to the service, whether they are hosted on WP Engine or another hosting platform. Developers can also use the GraphQL API directly to build custom indexing and search integrations.

This page explains how the primary components of Smart Search AI work together so you can choose the appropriate integration approach.

## Architecture overview

[](#architecture-overview)

![Smart Search Architecture Diagram](/_astro/smart-search-architecture.BjfFCAw7_Z1JU1W.webp)

-   **Smart Search AI back end** - A cloud-based service that handles all search requests and responses via its GraphQL API. It indexes content, processes queries, and returns relevant results.
-   **Elasticsearch** - The underlying search engine. Elasticsearch provides scalable, reliable, real-time search and analytics capabilities.
-   **Vertex AI API** - Provides multimodal search capabilities. Smart Search AI uses the Vertex AI API to process different content types — including text, images, and other media — so that natural language queries return results across content types.
-   **WordPress plugin** - Integrates Smart Search AI into WordPress. Administrators can configure search settings, customize results, and connect the plugin to their WordPress site. The plugin communicates with the Smart Search AI back end via the GraphQL API.

## WordPress plugin

[](#wordpress-plugin)

The Smart Search AI plugin provides the following capabilities for WordPress sites:

1.  **Content indexing** - The plugin automatically indexes content from your WordPress site, including posts, pages, and custom post types; including content from Advanced Custom Fields (ACF), WooCommerce, and [other compatible plugins](https://wpengine.com/support/wp-engine-smart-search/#toc-compatibility-testing-for-popular-plugins), keeping content searchable and up-to-date in the Smart Search AI back end.
    
2.  **Admin controls** - The plugin provides an admin interface for configuring search settings, customizing results, and managing indexing on your WordPress site.
    
3.  **Front-end blocks** - The plugin ships Gutenberg blocks that can be added to any page or post. [Faceted blocks](https://wpengine.com/support/wp-engine-smart-search/#toc-faceted-gutenberg-blocks-for-smart-search) add filterable search interfaces with faceted navigation. [Recommendation blocks](https://wpengine.com/support/wp-engine-smart-search/#toc-recommendations-gutenberg-block-for-smart-search) surface related content independently of search.
    
4.  **API integration** - The plugin replaces WordPress’s default SQL-based search by hooking into native WordPress actions and filters (such as `pre_get_posts` and `posts_search`). This redirects all standard search queries — including those from `WP_Query`, the REST API (`/wp/v2/search`), and theme search forms — to the Smart Search AI back end. Smart Search AI functionality is also available via [WPGraphQL](https://wpengine.com/support/wp-engine-smart-search/#toc-querying-with-wp-engine-smart-search) and the [REST API](https://developer.wordpress.org/rest-api/) for headless and custom integrations.
    
5.  **Recommendations analytics** - The Smart Search AI back end collects and analyzes anonymized user interactions via an opt-in tracking script to surface recommendations based on trending content. Data collection is disabled by default.
    

## Beyond the plugin (custom integrations)

[](#beyond-the-plugin-custom-integrations)

The WordPress plugin runs entirely on the Smart Search AI GraphQL API. You can use the API directly to build search experiences on any platform, framework, or data source — not just WordPress.

1.  **Third-party data** - Index and search content from third-party systems, such as external databases, content management systems, or other data sources, alongside or independently of WordPress content.
2.  **Headless WordPress** - If you are using WordPress as a headless CMS, build custom search interfaces in your front-end application while maintaining full control over the user experience.
3.  **Custom applications** - Build custom search interfaces on any platform or framework, including mobile, web, and desktop applications.

[Getting Started with Smart Search API](/docs/smart-search/getting-started/)Authenticate and make your first request to the Smart Search AI GraphQL API.

name: RAG chatbot example
Getting Started
markdown:
This tutorial will walk you through authenticating with the Smart Search GraphQL API and making your first search request.

## Prerequisites

[](#prerequisites)

This tutorial assumes you have a Smart Search AI instance set up and running. If you haven’t done so already, please follow the [Smart Search AI Setup Guide](https://wpengine.com/support/wp-engine-smart-search/) to create your instance.

## Authentication Credentials

[](#authentication-credentials)

All API requests must be authenticated by sending a key (a.k.a. “Token”) in the `Authorization` header as a Bearer token.

```
Authorization: Bearer {your-api-key}
```

Find your credentials in the WP Engine User Portal, and save them securely.

-   [WP Engine Hosted](#tab-panel-0-0)
-   [Non-WP Engine Hosted](#tab-panel-0-1)

1.  Go to [my.wpengine.com/products/smart\_search](https://my.wpengine.com/products/smart_search)
2.  _Open_ the 3-dot menu for your site
3.  _Select_, “Show Credentials”
4.  _Save_, “URL” - This is the URL you will use to send your GraphQL requests.
5.  _Save_, “Access Token” - A private token used to authenticate your requests.

  

**You should now have saved info that looks like this:**

Credential

Example Value

GraphQL Endpoint

`https://{site_slug}-{short_id}-atlassearch-{unique_id}-uc.a.run.app/graphql`

Access Token

`00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000000`

Tip

For applications that perform searches, a `Search Token` is also available in the WP Engine User Portal. This token is restricted to search actions and cannot be used for mutative operations like indexing or deleting documents; making it safe to use in public-facing code.

Danger

**Treat your `Access Token` like a password.** It is private and grants full access to your environment’s data. Do not share it, publish it, or commit it to public repositories, code samples, or support forums.

1.  _Go_ to [my.wpengine.com/products/smart\_search\_per\_site](https://my.wpengine.com/products/smart_search_per_site)
2.  _Open_ the 3-dot menu for your site
3.  _Select_, “API site credentials”
4.  _Save_ the “API URL” - This is the URL you will use to send your GraphQL requests.
5.  _Select_, “Manage API Keys” from the modal
6.  _Select_, “Generate new Credentials” to create a new “Full access” key
7.  _Save_ this API key for use in the next step. This is your private access token.

  

**You should now have saved info that looks like this:**

Credential

Example Value

GraphQL Endpoint

`https://api.ai.wpengine.com/v1/smart-search/{instance-name}/graphql`

Full Access Key

`wpe_exampleFullAccessKey1234567890`

Tip

For applications that only perform searches, a `Read only` key is also available in the WP Engine User Portal. This token is restricted to search actions and cannot be used for mutative operations like indexing or deleting documents; making it safe to use in public-facing code.

Danger

**Treat your `Full Access` key like a password.** It is private and grants full access to your environment’s data. Do not share it, publish it, or commit it to public repositories, code samples, or support forums.

## Making your first request

[](#making-your-first-request)

You can make requests to the GraphQL endpoint using any HTTP client or dedicated GraphQL client.

This is an example of a basic `find` query using `curl` from the terminal of your choice.

-   [WP Engine Hosted](#tab-panel-1-0)
-   [Non-WP Engine Hosted](#tab-panel-1-1)

Replace `<your-smart-search-url>` with your unique GraphQL endpoint and `<your-access-token>` with your access token.

```
# This request performs a simple search for "hello world" and will return the total number of matching documents.
$ curl -X POST \  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \  -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-access-token>" \  --data '{ "query": "query { find(query: \"hello world\") { total } }" }' \  <your-smart-search-url>
```

```
// The response will look like this:
{  "data": {    "find": {      "total": 123    }  }}
```

Replace `<your-api-url>` with your unique API URL and `<your-api-key>` with your API key.

```
# This request performs a simple search for "hello world" and will return the total number of matching documents.
$ curl -X POST \  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \  -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-api-key>" \  --data '{ "query": "query { find(query: \"hello world\") { total } }" }' \  <your-api-url>
```

```
// The response will look like this:
{  "data": {    "find": {      "total": 123    }  }}
```

Tip

If you’re looking for a graphical interface to test your queries, popular choices include [Hoppscotch](https://hoppscotch.io/), [Postman](https://www.postman.com/), [Insomnia](https://insomnia.rest/), or [Bruno](https://www.usebruno.com/).

## Programmatic requests

[](#programmatic-requests)

You can also send Smart Search GraphQL requests directly from your application code.

-   [JavaScript (Node.js)](#tab-panel-2-0)
-   [Python](#tab-panel-2-1)

Use this example with Node.js v18+ (built-in `fetch`) or modern browser environments.

```
const GQL_ENDPOINT = '{your-smart-search-url}';const API_KEY = '{your-api-key}';
async function search(queryText) {  const response = await fetch(GQL_ENDPOINT, {    method: 'POST',    headers: {      'Content-Type': 'application/json',      Authorization: `Bearer ${API_KEY}`,    },    body: JSON.stringify({      query: `        query FindQuery($query: String!) {          find(query: $query) {            total            documents {              id              data            }          }        }      `,      variables: {        query: queryText,      },    }),  });
  if (!response.ok) {    throw new Error(`Request failed with status ${response.status}`);  }
  const result = await response.json();  console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2));}
search('hello world').catch(console.error);
```

This example uses the `requests` package.

```
import jsonimport requests
GQL_ENDPOINT = "{your-smart-search-url}"API_KEY = "{your-api-key}"
def search(query_text):    headers = {        "Content-Type": "application/json",        "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",    }
    payload = {        "query": """            query FindQuery($query: String!) {                find(query: $query) {                    total                    documents {                        id                        data                    }                }            }        """,        "variables": {            "query": query_text        }    }
    response = requests.post(        GQL_ENDPOINT,        headers=headers,        data=json.dumps(payload),        timeout=30,    )    response.raise_for_status()    print(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))

search("hello world")
```

## Next steps

[](#next-steps)

Now that you know how to authenticate and make a basic request, you can explore the full capabilities of the API. For a complete guide to all available parameters, operators, and advanced features, please see the individual API pages.

#### Smart Search API reference guides

-   [Index API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/indexing/)
-   [Find API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/find/)
-   [Recommendations API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/recommendations/)
-   [Semantic Search Config API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/semantic-search-config/)
-   [Synonyms API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/synonyms/)
-   [Content Extraction API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/content-extraction-api/)
-   [Insights API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/insights/)
-   [MCP Server](/docs/smart-search/mcp/)

name: Content Extraction API
markdown:
This API and its endpoints are in BETA.

Beta Services as described by Section 2.e. of the terms of services located [here](https://wpengine.com/legal/terms-of-service/)

The Content Extraction API provides AI-powered tools to extract and analyze content from various file types:

-   **PDF Extraction** - Extract text content and metadata from PDF documents
-   **Image Analysis** - Generate descriptions, captions, and alt text for images using AI

Both APIs support multiple input sources:

-   Public URLs
-   Base64-encoded data

## PDF Extraction

[](#pdf-extraction)

Extract text content from PDF documents for indexing, analysis, or content management.

### Basic PDF Extraction

[](#basic-pdf-extraction)

```
query ExtractPDF {  pdf {    extract(input: { source: "https://example.com/document.pdf" }) {      source      content      pageCount      metadata      processedAt    }  }}
```

### PDF Extraction with Base64

[](#pdf-extraction-with-base64)

```
query ExtractPDFFromBase64 {  pdf {    extract(      input: {        source: "data:application/pdf;base64,JVBERi0xLjQKJeLjz9MKMSAwIG9iago8..."        meta: {          action: "extract"          system: "content-management"          source: "upload-form"        }      }    ) {      source      content      pageCount      metadata      processedAt    }  }}
```

### PDF Extraction Response

[](#pdf-extraction-response)

The extraction returns:

-   **source** - The source that was processed (URL, file path, or “base64”)
-   **content** - Extracted text content from the PDF
-   **pageCount** - Number of pages in the PDF
-   **metadata** - Document metadata (file size, modification time, etc.)
-   **processedAt** - Timestamp when the extraction was processed

### Common Use Cases

[](#common-use-cases)

**Index PDF content for search:**

```
query ExtractPDFForIndexing {  pdf {    extract(input: { source: "https://example.com/whitepaper.pdf" }) {      content      pageCount    }  }}
```

After extraction, you can index the content using the [Index API](/docs/smart-search/graphql-api/indexing).

## Image Analysis

[](#image-analysis)

Generate AI-powered descriptions, captions, and alt text for images to improve accessibility and SEO.

### Basic Image Analysis

[](#basic-image-analysis)

```
query AnalyzeImage {  image {    analyze(input: { source: "https://example.com/photo.jpg" }) {      source      description      caption      altText      processedAt    }  }}
```

### Image Analysis with Base64

[](#image-analysis-with-base64)

```
query AnalyzeImageFromBase64 {  image {    analyze(      input: {        source: "data:image/jpeg;base64,/9j/4AAQSkZJRgABAQEAYABgAAD..."        meta: { action: "analyze", system: "media-library", source: "upload" }      }    ) {      source      description      caption      altText      processedAt    }  }}
```

### Image Analysis Response

[](#image-analysis-response)

The analysis returns:

-   **source** - The source that was analyzed (URL, file path, or “base64”)
-   **description** - Detailed description of the image content
-   **caption** - Concise caption suitable for social media or articles
-   **altText** - Brief alt text for accessibility and screen readers
-   **processedAt** - Timestamp when the analysis was processed

### Common Use Cases

[](#common-use-cases-1)

**Generate alt text for accessibility:**

```
query GenerateAltText {  image {    analyze(input: { source: "https://example.com/product-image.jpg" }) {      altText    }  }}
```

**Create social media captions:**

```
query GenerateSocialCaption {  image {    analyze(input: { source: "https://example.com/marketing-photo.jpg" }) {      caption      description    }  }}
```
